channel.title: Science News – Bias and Credibility - Article Feed
channel.description: Latest articles from Science News – Bias and Credibility (sciencenews.org)

item.title: Mosquitoes’ butt cells tell them when to stop biting
item.description: Mosquitoes stop feeding because signals from rectal cells tell them they’re full, offering a target for preventing human bites.

item.title: Check out 6 ways orchids use tricks to reproduce
item.description: This spring, these six orchids will lure pollinators with mimicry, scent or other unusual strategies.

item.title: How realistic is Project Hail Mary?
item.description: Ryan Gosling is on a mission to save the sun — and Earth — from star-killing microbes. Science News dissects the science behind the sci-fi movie.

item.title: Amid vaccine policy whiplash, here's how a pediatrician talks to families
item.description: A court ruling that blocks Trump administration vaccine policy is a win for science. But much work remains to rebuild trust in vaccines.

item.title: Science and armed conflict
item.description: Editor in chief Nancy Shute discusses how science and armed conflict have been intertwined throughout history, from the Greeks in 400 B.C. to the use of tear gas in the protests across the United States as recently as a few months ago.

item.title: Long nails don’t work on touchscreens. An experimental polish could help
item.description: Proton movement in the nail polish probably activates the touchscreen, but the formula isn’t ready to hit shelves yet.

item.title: Female giant rainforest mantises grow up to strike harder than males
item.description: Scientists tracked mantis strike force from youth to adulthood, showing females eventually hit far harder than males. Why is a mystery.

item.title: In a rare event, the moon got a massive new crater
item.description: A crater as wide as two American football fields formed in spring 2024, a size expected roughly once a century. A NASA orbiter got to watch.

item.title: Neandertals made antibacterial ointment, but may not have known it
item.description: A team of scientists re-created the way Neandertals made birch tar and found its antibacterial properties could fight off skin infections.

item.title: These insects fly with their legs. Physics explains how
item.description: Phantom crane flies change the angle of their splayed legs to increase or reduce drag, helping them navigate varying winds.
